Document Title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Step-Level Tool-Call Safety Evaluation in Industrial Control Systems
Authors: Z. Xue; X. He
Author Affiliations: School of Software & Microelectronics, Peking University, Beijing, China; Fujian Provincial Industrial Internet, Development Research Center, Fuzhou, China
Publication Title: 2026 6th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Industrial Technology Applications (AIITA)
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to operate industrial systems through structured tool calls to Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems interfaces. However, unsafe tool-call behaviors—arising from reasoning errors, contextual prompt injection, or explicit malicious requests—can directly lead to physical damage and safety incidents. Despite recent progress in agent safety, standardized benchmarks for evaluating step-level tool-call safety in industrial environments remain lacking. In this work, we present a guardrail-oriented dataset and benchmark for industrial LLM agents. We propose a three-mode safety taxonomy that distinguishes benign, injected-benign, and malicious requests, capturing both explicit attacks and covert contextual manipulations that induce unsafe behaviors in otherwise legitimate tasks. Based on this taxonomy, we construct a step-level dataset using a fully automated multi-agent pipeline that (i) generates industrial environments and tasks, (ii) injects structured contextual manipulations, (iii) samples tool-call trajectories, and (iv) assigns deterministic safety labels grounded in PLC constraints and industrial safety specifications. We further design a challenging cross-domain benchmark spanning six industrial domains, including water treatment, semiconductor manufacturing, pharmaceutical fermentation, oil refining, nuclear cooling, and food processing. The benchmark enforces domain-specific entity naming, realistic numeric values, and constraint mismatches where physical safety limits are stricter than PLC register bounds, enabling systematic evaluation of guardrail generalization under distribution shift. Experimental results show that strong instruction-tuned LLMs, while effective at handling explicitly malicious requests, struggle to detect unsafe behaviors induced by contextual prompt injection, revealing a critical blind spot in existing safety mechanisms. In contrast, a guardrail model fine-tuned on our dataset demonstrates substantially improved sensitivity to step-level safety violations, particularly in injected-benign scenarios, while maintaining robust performance against explicit attacks. These findings highlight the necessity of step-level supervision and the effectiveness of the proposed benchmark for developing reliable industrial agent guardrails. Our dataset and benchmark provide a standardized testbed for step-level tool-call safety in industrial LLM agents and establish a foundation for future research on safe and reliable autonomous industrial systems.

Document Title: A Minimal Model for Emergent Collective Behaviors in Autonomous Robotic Multiagent Systems
Authors: H. B. Jond
Author Affiliations: Department of Cybernetics, Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Czech Technical University in Prague, Prague, Czech Republic
Publication Title: IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems
Abstract: Collective behaviors such as swarming and flocking emerge from simple, decentralized interactions in biological systems. Existing models, such as Vicsek and Cucker-Smale, lack collision avoidance, whereas the Olfati-Saber model imposes rigid formations, limiting their applicability in swarm robotics. To address these limitations, this article proposes a minimal yet expressive model that governs agent dynamics using relative positions, velocities, and local density, modulated by two tunable parameters: the spatial offset and kinetic offset. The model achieves spatially flexible, collision-free behaviors that reflect naturalistic group dynamics. Furthermore, we extend the framework to cognitive autonomous systems, enabling energy-aware phase transitions between swarming and flocking through adaptive control parameter tuning. This cognitively inspired approach offers a robust foundation for real-world applications in multirobot systems, particularly autonomous aerial swarms.

Abstract: Real-time coordination of large-scale mobile robot swarms remains a challenging problem, particularly in dynamic and obstacle-rich environments. The primary limitation arises from the computational complexity of peragent path planning, which becomes intractable as the number of robots increases. This paper proposes a centroid-based cluster control framework that integrates adaptive k-means clustering with graph-based global routing. The method reduces computational complexity by performing global path planning only for cluster centroids, rather than for individual robots. Local control laws combine attractive forces toward cluster centroids with repulsive inter-agent interactions to ensure collision avoidance and compliance with velocity constraints. The approach is validated through simulations with up to 200 robots at a control rate of 20 Hz. Experimental results demonstrate up to 92% reduction in computation time compared to per-agent A* planning, while path elongation remains below 9%. The proposed framework provides a scalable and efficient solution for decentralized multi-robot coordination in real-time applications.

Abstract: Industrial Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) procedures play a vital role in preventing accidents resulting from the misfortune of a hazardous energy being released unexpectedly during any maintenance work. Abstract: With each space robotic mission, a team of specialists on ground is usually required to support the robot throughout its mission. When scaling from single robots to fleets of robots, this will no longer be a viable way of conducting missions. Instead, in order to operate more autonomously in complex scenarios and adapt to dynamically changing environments without relying on a team of human experts, robots must be able to create a mental model of their surroundings. The relevance of this requirement becomes especially salient in the Surface Avatar ISS-to-ground telerobotic technology demonstration mission, where astronauts onboard the International Space Station command a team of heterogeneous robots in our lab. This work focuses on the final Surface Avatar session with NASA astronaut Jonny Kim where he was tasked with commanding the robots in a collaborative manner in order to complete simulated science and exploration tasks. To equip a complex robot such as DLR's Rollin' Justin with the ability to collaborate and coordinate with other robots, we deploy a combination of models and heuristics that allow it to create a mental model of its environment including its surrounding agents. Rollin' Justin also shares the estimated states generated in the mental model with the other robots. In this paper, we describe the application of this concept to our space experiment, present the models used to create the mental model, and evaluate it based on data collected in the final Surface Avatar experiment.

Author Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Nagaoka University of Technology, Nagaoka, Niigata, Japan; Department of Mechanical Engineering, Nagaoka University of Technology, Nagaoka, Niigata, Japan; Department of Mechanical Engineering and Science, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan; Department of Mechanical Engineering, Nagaoka University of Technology, Nagaoka, Niigata, Japan
Publication Title: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
Abstract: This paper presents a distributed navigation algorithm for robotic swarm systems based on model predictive control (MPC). The proposed algorithm addresses sudden robot failures, in which a robot suddenly comes to a halt due to hardware malfunctions or similar causes. Such failures may disrupt swarm connectivity and hinder mission execution, requiring navigation strategies that enable continued swarm operation. The proposed approach considers a leader–follower scenario in which a leader guides follower robots. Each follower determines its motion using only local information from robots within its sensing range, while satisfying practical constraints such as maximum sensing distance and speed. Within a distributed MPC framework, each robot autonomously performs collision avoidance, connectivity maintenance, connectivity recovery after failures, and connectivity strengthening. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method enables the swarm to restore connectivity after failure and continue navigation while avoiding collisions, even when a failed robot remains in the environment as an obstacle. Note to Practitioners—Robotic swarms are increasingly considered for tasks such as warehouse transport, infrastructure inspection, and environmental monitoring. In such environments, individual robots may unexpectedly stop because of hardware faults, battery depletion, or physical damage. A stopped robot may block nearby robots and break the local links needed for coordination, which can prevent the swarm from completing its task. Practical swarm systems, therefore, require navigation strategies that allow continued operation under such failures. The navigation approach presented in this paper enables a robotic swarm to continue operating when a robot suddenly stops and remains in the workspace as an obstacle. Each robot, other than the leader, determines its motion based only on nearby robot information, without relying on centralized coordination or global communication. With the proposed navigation strategy, robots can avoid collisions, maintain connectivity, recover lost links caused by a failed robot, and reinforce connectivity while moving around the failed robot. The current study assumes relatively simple robot dynamics and focuses on failures in which a robot becomes stationary. Future work is needed to address more complex robot dynamics, larger robot populations, and broader classes of failures.

Abstract: Autonomous robotics is transitioning from deterministic automation towards systems capable of reasoning and cooperation. Yet the dominant model treats AI as a tool, where the robot provides the body and the AI provides control. This paper argues this model is inadequate for substrate-independent, anorganic intelligence. We propose a transition to organic-anorganic cognitive partnership, where the embedded intelligence is an active participant in perception and decision-making. We present a three-tier architecture: individual anorganic intelligence within a robot, coordination among multiple intelligences, and human-AI symbiosis. The PAM multi-agent system serves as an experimental model for this coordination, demonstrating how differentiated agents can share memory and resolve conflict. This leads to design implications including shared cognitive memory, dialogue-oriented communication, and offline processing for cognitive consolidation. We argue that genuinely autonomous systems require architectural support for regulation and reflection, not just task execution. Within the framework of Anorganology, this shifts the design question from command execution to how organic and anorganic intelligences can reason and evolve together. This transition provides a foundation for a more mature, co-evolutionary form of autonomous robotics.

Abstract: In multi-robot systems operating in shared environments, avoiding collisions while maintaining efficiency remains a critical challenge. This paper proposes a decentralized real-time collision-avoidance framework that integrates trajectory prediction, collision risk detection, success probability evaluation with Bayesian Networks, and a distributed consensus mechanism. When a potential collision is detected, robots generate candidate velocity strategies and evaluate their success probabilities. Robots exchange these probabilities and select the velocity combination with the highest combined success probability through distributed consensus. Simulation experiments in a Gazebo environment demonstrate that the proposed approach enables robots to coordinate their velocities and safely pass through intersection regions. Since the framework relies only on local information exchange without a centralized controller, it demonstrates strong scalability and applicability for decentralized multi-robot systems.

Abstract: Intelligent fire response systems are essential for autonomous warehouses, as they must anticipate how the fire will spread and automatically direct suppression efforts to protect assets and minimize disruption to operations. Traditional fire detection and alarm systems, which rely on threshold detection and centralized control, have restrictions in terms of their predictive ability and their ability to coordinate the use of resources. A hybrid architecture is suggested in this research paper which integrates two architectures, the first is the fire spread prediction capability of Cellular Automata (CA) and the second is the fire intelligent resource allocation capability of Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (CMARL). The fire risk prediction goes into a Dynamic Fire Risk Prioritization Module (DFRPM) that enables prioritization of emergency response, based on the estimated fire propagation, amount of hazardous materials, value of assets, and accessibility of the zone. The decentralized CMARL agents coordinate sprinklers, fire doors, smoke ventilation systems and emergency alarms according to prioritized risk by using Cooperative Resource Allocation Module (CRAM). The resource allocation problem is defined as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) problem to enable cooperative action on the basis of local observation and communication between agents. The proposed framework is tested in an experimental application in a simulated warehouse of dimensions 50 m × 50 m, and the results demonstrate that it can be used to significantly lower the containment time, burned area, water consumption and resource conflicts compared to the traditional fire response methods. The proposed framework is scalable and applicable to smart warehouses, logistics centers, automated storage systems, and hazardous-material facilities, supporting SDG 9 and SDG 11 through efficient fire safety and emergency response.

Abstract: Wearable technologies have become pivotal for enhancing human–machine interaction and safety within the Industry 5.0 paradigm. This review assesses recent developments in wearable sensor technology, emphasizing their evolution from passive protective equipment into sophisticated active systems capable of delivering real-time monitoring, adaptive feedback, and proactive risk management. Key wearable applications explored in this article include physiological monitoring, environmental hazard detection, ergonomic optimization, and intelligent assistive interactions. Despite substantial progress, significant research gaps persist, particularly in wearable-enabled real-time actuation capabilities, personalized adaptive intelligence integration, and collaborative multiagent frameworks. Abstract: Recently, multi-robot systems have gained significant attention for their promise of scalable efficiency, reliability, and cost savings. Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has shown promise for multi-robot coordination, but its use in safety-critical systems requires reliable constraint handling. Trigger-aware experience replay (TAER) assigns higher training priority to safety-critical transitions identified by CBF interventions, encouraging the policy to avoid hazardous regions. Traditional methods usually treat task planning and motion planning as two independent processes, which makes it difficult to fully consider the dynamic constraints of the robot’s actual motion during the task allocation stage, resulting in frequent collisions and other issues during execution. To address this challenge, this study constructs a unified framework based on hierarchical reinforcement learning, which achieves efficient collaboration of multi-robot systems through collaborative optimization of task planning and motion planning. Future work will focus on studying the adaptability of this method in dynamic task environments and further expanding its application potential in diverse industrial scenarios.

Abstract: Language is one of the most intuitive ways for humans to communicate intent or corrections, however, translating high-level open-vocabulary instructions into reliable robot spatial motion adaptations is far from trivial. Language instructions are typically contextual, without the spatial precision required for robot execution, while the resulting motion must simultaneously respect geometric, kinematic, and environmental conditions. This becomes particularly challenging when several instructions interact or impose conflicting spatial requirements, spatial relationships that are not necessarily apparent to the user when expressing them. To bridge this gap, we present GELATO, a language-driven trajectory-reshaping framework that explicitly unifies semantic interpretation with geometric scene reasoning, connecting high-level user intent to verifiable robot-motion adaptations. GELATO automatically constructs a semantic–geometric representation of the environment by registering scene objects as 6D analytic primitives through a VLM-assisted multi-view pipeline. An LLM translates free-form instructions into explicit geometric and kinematic conditions tied to these representations, which are incorporated into a geometry-aware vector-field optimisation for trajectory reshaping. A multi-agent orchestration further explores such geometrically verifiable conditions together with complementary ways of resolving interacting instructions, while an Observer–Refinement loop verifies the resulting motion, checks constraint satisfaction, and adjusts failed candidates, increasing the success rate without retraining. Simulated, user studies, and real-world quantitative results demonstrate that our method achieves smoother, safer, and more reliable solutions compared to state-of-the-art baselines, with a high success rate on complex multi-instruction examples. Note to Practitioners—Robots are increasingly deployed near people in homes, care settings, and flexible workspaces, where users need intuitive ways to modify and correct their motion without reprogramming the system. In such scenarios, a practical challenge is to interpret multiple natural-language instructions, often conflicting, and convert them into reliable, context-aware, collision-free trajectory adaptations. GELATO addresses this problem through a modular, open-vocabulary framework for multi-instruction trajectory reshaping. Using off-the-shelf RGB-D cameras and vision models, it automatically registers scene objects as 6D analytic primitives, enabling more interpretable and predictable trajectory updates than point-based alternatives. It further introduces a multi-agent orchestration strategy that explores complementary ways of resolving interacting instructions, providing broader coverage of the solution space rather than a single strategy alone. By mapping language into explicit geometric constraints and reasoning over object pose and primitive shapes, GELATO generates, verifies, and refines multiple trajectory modifications, ensuring the users intent is satisfied while maintaining safe clearances. In practice, this provides a reliable way to deploy human-guided robots without retraining or requiring users to have programming expertise, offering a practical reference for more intuitive collaboration in industrial and service robotics.

Abstract: The design of decision mechanisms significantly impacts consensus generation in multi-agent systems (MAS), yet few computational frameworks have systematically evaluated these protocols in complex, asymmetric environments where agents possess heterogeneous decision-making power. Abstract: The Colored Traveling Salesman Problem (CTSP) is a seminal generalization of the Multiple TSP, where colors represent the heterogeneity of salesmen and their city visits. Combined with a truncated tree search, this facilitates efficient beam-guided exploration. Extensive experiments validate the proposed formulation and demonstrate that BeamVNS outperforms baseline methods adapted for T-CTSP. Finally, T-CTSP and BeamVNS are applied to multi-robot 3D printing and rebar mesh welding, proving their effectiveness in optimizing complex robotic manufacturing processes. The proposed time-critical colored traveling salesman problem provides a unified mathematical formulation that simultaneously captures routing decisions, temporal coordination, and safety-distance constraints. The beam variable neighborhood search is developed to address the large-scale T-CTSP instances. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BeamVNS can provide high-quality and safety-aware operational plans for decision-makers. For practitioners, this framework can serve as a planning tool for multi-robot task scheduling and path planning in manufacturing and automation systems. Case studies in multi-robot 3D printing and rebar mesh welding further verify that the proposed approach effectively ensures collision avoidance among robots and significantly improves operational efficiency.

Abstract: Aiming at the challenges in planning for the synchronized execution of multiple geometrically heterogeneous tasks by swarms in uncertain environments, this work proposes a distributed task planning method. This method is intended to overcome the inefficiencies in traditional methods caused by fragmented task modeling, high sensitivity to environmental uncertainty, and the risk of collaborative deadlocks. First, a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) model is introduced to dynamically estimate task execution time under uncertainty. Second, multi-geometry tasks (area, line, point) are uniformly transformed into equivalent point-task sets via grid-based decomposition and key-point discretization. Finally, a cooperative task dependency graph is embedded into a distributed auction consensus mechanism with cycle detection to prevent deadlocks, and an adaptive cooperative obstacle avoidance strategy based on task progress is integrated to ensure synchronized and collision-free motion. Simulation results demonstrate our method’s superiority over benchmarks in completion time, success rate, and efficiency. Its practicality is validated through real-world UAV tests, while scalability experiments confirm its robustness in large-scale scenarios. This work provides a solid theoretical foundation and technical support for efficient coordination of robot swarms in complex and dynamic environments. Note to Practitioners—Distributed task planning in multi-robot systems is essential for practical applications such as disaster response, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure inspection. These scenarios often involve uncertainties, diverse task geometries, and strict synchronization constraints, posing significant challenges to conventional algorithms. This paper introduces a robust and scalable planning framework that incorporates dynamic risk assessment, deadlock immunity, and cooperative motion planning. The proposed method supports efficient and safe execution of synchronized heterogeneous tasks under complex environmental conditions. Practitioners can adopt this approach to improve the coordination of autonomous aerial or ground vehicle swarms, particularly in scenarios where real-time responsiveness and high task success rates are critical. Future work may focus on hardware integration and communication robustness for field deployment.

Abstract: This letter addresses the collision-free planning problem for heterogeneous multi-agent systems. Abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents has introduced a largely uncharacterized attack surface in production AI deployments. Unlike static model inference, agentic pipelines expose dynamic execution paths, persistent memory, and third-party tool integrations that adversaries can exploit through carefully crafted inputs. This paper presents a structured threat model for autonomous LLM agents operating in cybersecurity-sensitive environments. The research objective is to identify, formalize, and mitigate attack vectors unique to agentic LLM pipelines that existing security frameworks fail to address. We formalize five primary attack vectors: prompt injection chaining, tool misuse via intent manipulation, goal drift through context poisoning, memory persistence exploitation, and cross-agent trust escalation. We provide empirical demonstrations using three publicly available agentic frameworks—AutoGPT, LangChain, and CrewAI—and propose CyberShield-A, a three-layer containment architecture comprising input sanitization, execution sandboxing, and behavioral auditing. Evaluation across 47 red-team scenarios demonstrates that CyberShield-A reduces successful attack completion rates by 73.4% while preserving 91.2% task utility. A full 2^3 ablation study confirms that all three layers contribute independently significant protection (p<0.001 for each). These findings establish a foundational taxonomy and deployable architecture for securing the next generation of autonomous AI systems.

Abstract: The collective behavior of a swarm forms from the emergent properties of local agent interactions. These interaction rules, while often simple, are difficult to craft by hand. Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents that plan, use tools and act has begun to shape healthcare and medicine. Reported studies demonstrate competence on various tasks ranging from EHR analysis and differential diagnosis to treatment planning and research workflows. We address this by reviewing 49 studies using a seven-dimensional taxonomy: Cognitive Capabilities, Knowledge Management, Interaction Patterns, Adaptation & Learning, Safety & Ethics, Framework Typology and Core Tasks & Subtasks with 29 operational sub-dimensions. Using explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria and a labeling rubric (Fully Implemented ✓, Partially Implemented  $\Delta $ , Not Implemented ✗), we map each study to the taxonomy and report quantitative summaries of capability prevalence and co-occurrence patterns. Our empirical analysis surfaces clear asymmetries. For instance, the External Knowledge Integration sub-dimension under Knowledge Management is commonly realized (~76% ✓) whereas Event-Triggered Activation sub-dimenison under Interaction Patterns is largely absent (~92% ✗) and Drift Detection & Mitigation sub-dimension under Adaptation & Learning is rare (~98% ✗). Architecturally, Multi-Agent Design sub-dimension under Framework Typology is the dominant pattern (~82% ✓) while orchestration layers remain mostly partial. Across Core Tasks & Subtasks, information centric capabilities lead e.g., Medical Question Answering & Decision Support and Benchmarking & Simulation, while action and discovery oriented areas such as Treatment Planning & Prescription still show substantial gaps (~59% ✗). Together, these findings provide an empirical baseline indicating that current agents excel at retrieval-grounded advising but require stronger adaptation and compliance platforms to move from early-stage systems to dependable systems.

Abstract: Multiagent path finding (MAPF) is a critical problem in real-world multiagent systems, where agents reach their respective destinations without colliding with one another. Next, safe learning under saturation limits is guaranteed through a safety-aware cost function. We establish safety, optimality, and stability properties (novel) in a mathematically rigorous manner. Furthermore, the safe RL problem is solved in an off-policy manner, and neural networks are used to approximate the value function and the control policy. To that end, we establish a novel off-policy equation under input saturation. Finally, simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework.

Abstract: The next-generation wireless technologies, including beyond 5G and 6G networks, are paving the way for transformative applications such as vehicle platooning, smart cities, and remote surgery. These innovations are driven by a vast array of interconnected wireless entities, including IoT devices, access points, UAVs, and CAVs, which increase network complexity and demand more advanced decision-making algorithms. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), especially reinforcement learning (RL), are key enablers for such networks, providing solutions to high-dimensional and complex challenges. However, as networks expand to multi-agent environments, traditional online RL approaches face cost, safety, and scalability limitations. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a promising solution by utilizing pre-collected data, reducing the need for real-time interaction. This article introduces a novel offline MARL algorithm based on conservative Q-learning (CQL), ensuring safe and efficient training. We extend this with meta-learning to address dynamic environments and validate the approach through use cases in radio resource management and UAV networks. Our work highlights offline MARL’s advantages, limitations, and future directions in wireless applications.

Authors: S. Guha; A. Datta
Author Affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering, The University of Western Australia, Crawley, Australia; Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering, The University of Western Australia, Crawley, Australia
Publication Title: IEEE Access
Abstract: Early fault prediction in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT)-based predictive maintenance systems is typically framed as an end-to-end learning problem, where models map multivariate sensor windows directly to warning or failure labels. Although such approaches can achieve high recall, they often generate unstable alerts, excessive false alarms, and limited operational interpretability, which restricts their use in safety-critical settings. We introduce ASPIRE, a decision-centric multi-agent system that reframes early fault prediction as a structured decision problem under uncertainty. Instead of using model outputs as direct alert triggers, ASPIRE combines evidence from role-specialised agents that monitor local sensor anomalies, temporal regime shifts, and fault probabilities. This evidence is evaluated by a deterministic Decision Agent using explicit and auditable policies, including margin-based gating and contextual evidence. In doing so, ASPIRE separates prediction from operational decision-making without modifying or retraining the underlying predictive model. Evaluated on the MetroPT-3 dataset for two-hour-ahead early-warning prediction and fault detection, ASPIRE improves early-warning precision from 0.875 to 0.889, recall from 0.941 to 0.953, and F1-score from 0.906 to 0.920 over a strong Transformer baseline, while maintaining identical fault-detection performance. Agreement-bucket and ablation analyses indicate that these gains are driven by two decision-layer mechanisms: suppression of ambiguous boundary-adjacent warnings through margin-based gating, and recovery of near-miss cases using window-level temporal context evidence from the Adaptive Window Agent. A non-intervening LLM-based Expert Agent provides human-readable explanations and recommended operator actions without influencing automated decisions. Overall, the results show that treating decision-making as a core component of the system improves reliability, interpretability, and robustness under changing operating conditions. A cost-efficiency and cost-effectiveness analysis further shows that ASPIRE’s performance gains can translate into operational cost benefits, even when exact preventive intervention or breakdown costs are unknown.

Abstract: This paper addresses distributed predefined-time adaptive tracking control for a class of nonlinear multi-agent systems (MASs) with unknown dynamics and external disturbances, subject to prescribed-performance constraints on coordination tracking errors. A smooth self-regulating prescribed-performance control framework is developed to mitigate the feasibility conflict between rapidly shrinking performance envelopes and fast convergence requirements. Specifically, a differentiable self-regulating performance boundary is constructed via hyperbolic tangent functions to relax the constraint near the boundary, thereby preventing transformation singularities and alleviating chattering. A practical predefined-time control law is then designed to drive the coordination tracking errors into a tunable residual set within a user-specified time, regardless of initial conditions. To compensate lumped uncertainties without requiring acceleration measurements, a predefined-time nonlinear disturbance observer (PTNDO) is introduced using only velocity information. In addition, a dynamic event-triggered mechanism (DETM) is incorporated to reduce inter-agent communications and controller updates while excluding Zeno behavior. Lyapunov-based analysis proves boundedness of all closed-loop signals and practical predefined-time stability under the proposed scheme. Simulation results demonstrate fast convergence, satisfaction of the proposed self-regulated performance bounds, and reduced triggering frequency. Note to Practitioners—This paper investigates distributed predefined-time consensus control for nonlinear multi-agent systems subject to performance constraints. In engineering applications such as UAV swarms, achieving rapid convergence within a strictly defined time is crucial. However, aggressive convergence requirements often conflict with rigid safety constraints, potentially leading to controller singularity or oscillation. To address this practical issue, a self-regulating constraint framework is developed to automatically adjust boundaries, thereby ensuring smooth control signals and avoiding singularities. Furthermore, considering the limited communication bandwidth and unknown disturbances in real-world networked environments, a dynamic event-triggered mechanism and a velocity-based disturbance observer are integrated. This approach effectively reduces the communication burden and compensates for disturbances without requiring acceleration measurements. However, practitioners should note that this approach currently relies on velocity measurements, and high-frequency noise could affect the observer’s accuracy. Future work will focus on validating this algorithm on physical hardware testbeds and extending it to scenarios with significant communication delays.

Abstract: This letter proposes a distributed model predictive control (DMPC) method for multi-agent systems with smooth nonlinear dynamics and constraints, including pairwise distance constraints for collision avoidance. Publication Title: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Vehicles
Abstract: Continuous operation of automated guided vehicles (AGVs) in intelligent factories is often interrupted by battery depletion and additional travel to fixed charging stations. Although wireless power transfer (WPT) can reduce physical connector wear and enable flexible charging, its use for AGV energy support must account for charging efficiency loss, uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) hovering consumption, propulsion energy, and operational safety constraints. This work develops a physically parameterized hybrid aerial-ground energy-management framework in which UAVs equipped with WPT modules (UWs) provide supplementary and on-demand charging support to AGV fleets. The coupled UW-AGV charging mission is formulated as an episodic Markov decision process. To support real-time decision-making, a feature-based expected SARSA (FES) algorithm is developed to compress the state-action space through five problem-specific feature functions associated with energy cost, downtime penalty, charging efficiency, spatial proximity, and battery-safety margin. The proposed model explicitly incorporates WPT efficiency, UAV hovering energy, and propulsion-related energy consumption. Simulation experiments compare the proposed FES algorithm with feature-based SARSA, rule-based, and random baselines, and further analyze convergence behavior, computational scalability, UW deployment density, and the sensitivity of system performance to WPT efficiency, UW hovering or docking-maintenance power, and propulsion energy. The results show that FES provides computationally efficient and interpretable scheduling for hybrid AGV-UAV energy coordination, while limitations of large-scale UAV-assisted WPT deployment are explicitly discussed.

Abstract: As agentic AI systems gain autonomy and self-optimization capabilities; they increasingly operate within complex feedback loops that can lead to unexpected emergent behaviors.
